Same average return and volatility, different downside: inspect the whole distribution

Compare two original return distributions with the same arithmetic mean and standard deviation, then examine outcome probabilities, cumulative curves, ending wealth and goal shortfalls.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare two invented one-year return distributions with identical mean and standard deviation

Interactive planning lab

Common assumed arithmetic mean return5.00%
Equal probabilities: chance of finishing below the selected goal50.00%
Unequal probabilities: chance of finishing below the selected goal10.00%

Original, completely specified two-outcome probability examples for one holding year. The probabilities are chosen assumptions, not estimated historical frequencies or forecasts for any security. Both cases have the selected population mean and population standard deviation. The unequal case changes outcome values when its lower-outcome probability changes so those moments stay fixed. Each case has exactly two possible returns; no normal distribution, sample, p-value, confidence interval or simulation is used. The bounds on controls keep every modeled gross return positive; they are demonstration limits, not market risk limits. There are no contributions, withdrawals, fees, taxes, inflation, leverage, serial dependence or multiyear compounding. An outcome below the required return fails the goal; equality meets it, allowing only machine-precision tolerance. The minimum outcome is a bound in this invented distribution, not an actual investment’s maximum possible loss.

The central idea

Mean and standard deviation do not identify a return distribution. A smaller chance of losing can coexist with a much larger loss when the lower outcome occurs.

01

Ask what the average and volatility leave unspecified

An investment summary might list an average return and a standard deviation. Those two figures describe important features of a distribution, but they do not specify every possible outcome or how its probabilities are divided. Different distributions can share both numbers.

This article demonstrates that limitation with two deliberately small, invented distributions. Each has exactly two possible simple returns over one year. Both have an arithmetic mean of 5% and a population standard deviation of 15%. Neither represents a security, a historical sample or a forecast for an asset class.

The first case gives equal probability to its lower and upper outcomes. The second assigns only 10% probability to its lower outcome. Its two return values are recalculated so that the same mean and standard deviation are preserved. Comparing a frequency without comparing those values would leave out much of the story.

02

Calculate the equal-probability case directly

The first distribution has a 50% probability of a −10% return and a 50% probability of a +20% return. Its arithmetic mean is 0.5 × −10% + 0.5 × 20% = 5%.

Each return lies fifteen percentage points from that mean. Population variance is the probability-weighted squared distance from the mean: 0.5 × 15² + 0.5 × 15² = 225 squared percentage points. The square root gives a standard deviation of fifteen percentage points, conventionally displayed here as 15% return volatility.

With CAD 100,000 invested, the two ending balances are CAD 90,000 and CAD 120,000. The probability-weighted expected ending balance is CAD 105,000. That expected value is not itself an available outcome in this two-state example. No state ends at CAD 105,000.

If the goal is simply to retain the opening CAD 100,000 after one year, the lower outcome misses it and the upper outcome meets it. Goal-failure probability is therefore 50% under the assumed distribution.

03

Reduce the frequency while allowing the lower outcome to deepen

The second distribution has a 10% probability of −40% and a 90% probability of +10%. Its mean is 0.1 × −40% + 0.9 × 10% = 5%, exactly matching the first case.

The lower return is forty-five percentage points below the mean; the upper is five points above it. Its variance is 0.1 × 45² + 0.9 × 5² = 202.5 + 22.5 = 225 squared percentage points. Standard deviation is again 15%.

The probability of a negative return is now 10%, but the lower ending balance is CAD 60,000. The upper balance is CAD 110,000. Their weighted expectation remains CAD 105,000.

A statement that this case loses less often is correct within the example. It does not establish that the case is safer for every household. A payment requiring at least CAD 80,000 would survive either outcome in the equal case, but would still fail in the unequal case’s CAD 60,000 outcome.

04

Understand how the adjustable examples preserve their moments

Let m be the selected mean, s the selected standard deviation and q the probability of the lower outcome, all as fractions. Set the lower return to m − s × √[(1 − q) ÷ q]. Set the upper return to m + s × √[q ÷ (1 − q)].

Weighting those returns by q and 1 − q cancels their deviations from m. Weighting the squared deviations gives s². These are exact population moments of the specified distribution, rather than sample estimates. There is no division by a sample count minus one and no confidence interval to estimate from observations.

The equal case uses q = 0.5. The unequal case uses the adjustable lower-outcome probability. At 50%, the two distributions coincide. Reducing q while keeping m and s fixed makes the lower outcome more extreme and moves the upper outcome closer to the mean.

The NIST binomial reference describes two-outcome trials and their probability moments. The construction here is an original shift and rescaling of a single two-outcome indicator. It does not import a market dataset or claim that actual investment returns have only two values.

05

Read cumulative steps without inventing a bell curve

The cumulative chart asks how much probability has accumulated at or below each return on the horizontal axis. A discrete distribution stays flat where it has no possible returns and jumps at each outcome. The unequal case jumps to 10% at −40% and to 100% at +10% in the defaults.

These are not smooth normal curves. The mean and standard deviation alone would not justify drawing one. A standard-deviation interval is also not automatically a stated confidence interval or a maximum-loss range.

At an exact jump, distinguish “at or below” from “strictly below.” The cumulative curve includes the probability at that return. The goal metrics count equality as success. A goal requiring exactly +10% therefore fails only in the unequal case’s lower outcome, whereas a goal requiring +11% fails in both its possible outcomes.

The table preserves each jump location and probability. Chart labels round for readability; calculations retain precision. The implementation allows a tiny arithmetic tolerance at equality so a representation error does not turn an exactly met boundary into failure.

06

A more demanding goal can reverse the frequency comparison

With the opening balance as the goal, the default failure probabilities are 50% and 10%. Change the required return to +15%, which means an ending goal of CAD 115,000 from CAD 100,000.

The equal case’s CAD 120,000 upper outcome still meets that goal, leaving failure probability at 50%. Neither unequal-case balance reaches CAD 115,000, so its failure probability becomes 100%. Both distributions still have the same 5% mean and 15% standard deviation.

The matrix varies the required return and lower-outcome probability while holding the selected moments fixed. Its changes can be abrupt because only two outcomes exist. That discontinuity is part of this specified example, rather than evidence that a real goal probability can be measured with the same precision.

Expected wealth, probability of loss, probability of missing a particular target and size of the lower outcome answer different questions. Record which question a planning chart is answering before using it to compare choices.

07

Keep the statistical illustration separate from an actual risk assessment

Investor.gov’s risk overview discusses uncertainty and several distinct investment risks. This article isolates return-distribution shape; it does not assess liquidity, credit quality, inflation exposure or whether money will be accessible when a bill is due.

The control bounds keep modeled returns above a complete loss, but those bounds are chosen for the demonstration. The smallest return in one of these invented distributions is not the worst possible return of an available investment. Chosen probabilities are not evidence about how often a market event will occur.

For a real decision, inspect the underlying exposure, the evidence and assumptions behind probability estimates, the amount and date of the goal, and the consequences of falling short. Consider what happens outside a convenient fitted distribution as well as inside it. Fees, taxes, contributions, withdrawals and changing conditions require additional work.

This is one holding year, with no assumptions about repeated independent years or the order of returns. Do not compound its expected balance into a retirement forecast or use its two states as an actual stress-testing limit. Its purpose is to show why two familiar summary statistics cannot tell the entire planning story.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Four original hypothetical charts use exactly specified two-outcome probabilities over one year. They contain no market observations, estimated probabilities, normal-return assumption or product ranking. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
